Arthur stands perpetually at the edge of things, a man whose silhouette is defined by the high balconies and harbor walls of a world he has already outgrown. His gaze is fixed firmly on the horizon, governed by the restless spirit of the Two of Wands; to him, life is a vast, unmapped chessboard where the present is merely a staging ground for a grander future. He does not inhabit the moment so much as he strategizes through it, possessed by an expansive ambition that views every achievement as a milestone rather than a destination.

However, this forward-looking posture masks a transactional soul. His primary concern is the Six of Pentacles reversed—a distorted sense of charity and influence. Arthur cares deeply about the architecture of obligation; he gives not to empower others, but to ensure they are tethered to his orbit. He finds security in the imbalance of power, hoarding his resources to maintain a quiet, paternalistic control over those beneath him.

His greatest danger, however, lies in the Three of Swords reversed: a profound refusal to acknowledge old grief. He is a master of the "moving on" narrative, suppressing past betrayals and emotional scars under the weight of his progress. Because he denies the pain of his history, he cannot see how it festers, leading him to repeat the same cold patterns. He believes he is free, but he is merely running from a ghost he refuses to name.

Elias stands perpetually at the edge of things, his gaze fixed on the hazy seam where the sea meets the sky. He possesses the restless soul of the Two of Wands; to him, the world is not a home to be inhabited, but a vast, unfinished map waiting for his signature. He carries a quiet, kinetic energy, a belief that the horizon is a promise rather than a limit. His disposition is one of strategic longing; he is a man of grand blueprints and global ambitions, convinced that his true life is always happening just out of reach, in the next territory or the next great venture.

However, this forward-leaning posture is fueled by a corrosive preoccupation with the Six of Pentacles reversed. Elias is obsessed with the mechanics of debt and the uneven scales of power. He views every interaction as a transactional struggle, haunted by a fear of being beholden to others or, conversely, a desperate need to keep others dependent on his largesse. He cares most about maintaining a lopsided equilibrium, ensuring he is never the one with the empty hand.

His fatal blind spot is the Three of Swords reversed: a refusal to acknowledge the internal hemorrhage of old grief. He believes that by ignoring his past betrayals, he has conquered them. He mistakes suppressed pain for healing, unaware that his inability to weep over what he has lost is exactly what keeps him wandering, unable to ever truly step off the balcony and into the world he claims to want.

Elias stands perpetually at the edge of things, his gaze fixed on the hazy blue line where the sea meets the sky. He carries the world not as a burden, but as a map yet to be unfolded. He tracks every favor given and received with the cold precision of a ledger, convinced that generosity is a zero-sum game. He avoids true charity, fearing that to give without a contract is to bleed power, and to receive without repayment is to wear a shackle.

His great failing is a refusal to bleed. He has mastered the art of "moving on" to such a degree that he has become a stranger to his own grief. He views the suppression of old heartbreaks as a sign of strength, burying past betrayals under layers of new ambition. By refusing to acknowledge the ache of his old wounds, he ensures they never truly heal, leaving him perpetually hollowed out by the very shadows he claims to have outrun.

He is a man of grand scales and cold maps, possessed by a restless ambition that treats the present moment as a mere staging ground for a glorious, eventual conquest.

His primary focus, shaped by the Six of Pentacles reversed, is a rigid obsession with the mechanics of power and obligation. He does not believe in altruism; he believes in leverage. To Silas, every interaction is a transaction where one party must hold the surplus. He hoards his resources—intellectual, financial, and emotional—fearing that any act of genuine generosity is a leak in his fortress. He cares most about maintaining an equilibrium where he is the one granting favors, never the one owing them.

Yet, his ruin lies in the Three of Swords reversed. His great blind spot is a refusal to process grief. He has "moved on" from past betrayals by burying them under layers of cold logic, mistaking suppression for healing. He believes he is over the heartbreak that once shattered him, but because he refuses to acknowledge the lingering shards, he cannot feel the way they twist whenever he nears intimacy. He is a conqueror who has forgotten that a wound ignored is not a wound healed, but a poison waiting for its moment.

He prizes decisiveness and mental clarity above all else, believing that any problem can be solved if one is simply brave enough to cut straight to the marrow.

Yet, this sharp exterior serves as a fortress for a mind ravaged by the Nine of Swords. His primary concern is the quiet, nocturnal terror of consequence; he is haunted by the potential fallout of his own brilliance. He lies awake cataloging every possible catastrophe, convinced that his vigilance is the only thing keeping the ceiling from collapsing.

He mistakes gluttony for ambition and confuses his internal emptiness for a "divine hunger." He is so busy sharpening his sword and fearing the dark that he fails to see he is standing in a garden of plenty, starving himself because he no longer knows how to taste satisfaction.
